nameStory: The "elderberry" name comes from the Anglo-Saxon word "aeld," meaning fire, because the hollow stems were once used as bellows to blow air into fires. The "black" part distinguishes it from its red-berried cousin, referring to the deep purple-black clusters of berries that have been harvested for food and medicine for centuries.
description: American black elderberry is a fast-growing shrub that reaches 6-12 feet tall and wide, forming dense colonies through underground runners. It has a somewhat gangly, open growth habit with multiple stems arising from the base. The plant is famous for its flat-topped clusters of tiny white flowers in early summer, followed by drooping bunches of small dark purple berries. Its compound leaves give it a lush, tropical appearance despite being a hardy New England native.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Creamy white flowers form large, flat-topped clusters 4-8 inches across in early summer, with a sweet, honey-like fragrance that attracts clouds of pollinators

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 5-9 oval leaflets arranged like fingers on a hand, each leaflet 2-4 inches long with finely toothed edges and a smooth texture

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small dark purple-black berries in drooping clusters, each berry about 1/4 inch across with a slightly tart taste and purple juice that stains fingers

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Gray-brown bark with prominent warty bumps (lenticels) and soft, pithy white interior that's easily crushed between your fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Multi-stemmed shrub with somewhat arching branches and a tendency to form colonies, often looking a bit messy or wild compared to ornamental shrubs

habitat: Look for black elderberry in moist, rich soils along stream banks, pond edges, wetland borders, and roadside ditches throughout New England. It thrives in partial shade to full sun and often grows alongside red-osier dogwood, willows, and wild roses. You'll also find it in disturbed areas like old farm fields and forest clearings where the soil stays consistently moist.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green in late April to May, followed by the distinctive flat-topped flower clusters in June that fill the air with sweet fragrance.
seasonality.summer: Flowers give way to green berries that ripen to deep purple-black by late August, hanging in heavy drooping clusters that bend the branches downward.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow-green before dropping, and ripe berry clusters may persist into early fall, providing food for migrating birds.
seasonality.winter: Bare stems show the characteristic gray bark with warty bumps, and you can identify it by the soft, white pith inside broken twigs.

funFact: The flower clusters are so perfectly flat that people have traditionally used them as natural plates for serving food, and a single large shrub can produce up to 12,000 berries in a good year — enough to make gallons of elderberry syrup!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with red elderberry, but black elderberry has flat-topped white flower clusters (like a table) while red elderberry has dome-shaped yellowish flower clusters (like an umbrella). Remember: "Black is flat, red is a pyramid." The berries are also opposite colors — deep purple-black versus bright red.
contextualKnowledge: While elderberries are edible and prized for jams and syrups, the bark, leaves, and seeds contain compounds that can cause stomach upset, so only the ripe berries and cooked flowers should be consumed. This is one of the few wild berries that's actually better cooked than eaten raw.
compareHints: Compared to its relative red elderberry, American black elderberry grows larger, prefers wetter soils, and blooms later in the season. Red elderberry typically grows in shadier, more mountainous areas and has a more upright growth habit. Both have the same compound leaves and warty bark, but the flower and fruit colors are distinctly different.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red-berried elder differs from American black elderberry primarily in fruit color and cluster shape - red versus black berries, and pyramid-shaped versus flat-topped clusters.
